title: Traffic calming policy update with 25 priority streets
subtitle: Also: bring-your-own events delegation, taxi rate increase, water services report and staff recognitions.
overview: The committee recommended that Council approve an updated Traffic Calming Policy {{vote:m5}}. It focuses on 25 streets over five years, starting with community safety zones near schools and similar places. Staff said requests far exceed what staffing and budget can deliver, with more than 250 requests waiting. Those outstanding requests would be closed, and residents would be told. New requests could still be considered for other road safety measures, such as flex posts or radar boards. Council is expected to make the final decision later this month.

The committee also recommended that the City Clerk be given authority to designate community or cultural events for bring-your-own-event applications with the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario {{vote:m4}}. Staff stressed this does not allow people to bring alcohol to city parks. A special event permit is still required.

On the consent agenda, the committee recommended a 6.7 per cent increase in taxicab rates and received the 2025 water services reports. A councillor also announced a Ward 5 spring town hall on April 16 at Jean Little Public School.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the updated policy, which prioritizes 25 streets over five years, starting with community safety zones, and adds raised crossings to the available measures {{vote:m5}}.
The committee recommended amending the Delegation of Authority By-law so the City Clerk can designate events as community or cultural for bring-your-own-event applications {{vote:m4}}.
The committee recommended that staff amend the Taxicab By-law to raise taxicab rates by 6.7 per cent, effective April 1, 2026 or at the time of the City's meter check.
The committee received the 2025 Water Services Annual Report, the Summary Report and the Water Efficiency Strategy Progress Report.

debate: Delegates supported putting community safety zones first, citing parents' fear of fast traffic near schools and a recent fatal collision in the Junction neighbourhood. One delegate asked that the work be funded in upcoming budgets.

Several councillors questioned speed cushions. Concerns included noise, discomfort for people with chronic pain, and trike or cycle users who cannot avoid them in bike lanes. Staff said cushions let emergency vehicles and transit pass through, cost less than speed tables and reduce top-end speeds. They also said staff would look into speed tables.

Some councillors asked how residents will be treated once the backlog is closed. Staff said no new traffic calming studies are planned for the five-year list, but other tools remain available. Staff also committed to key messages for councillors and an updated web page and map.

One councillor who voted against said accessibility injuries are not being tracked and planned amendments before Council's final vote. Another councillor asked why a volume threshold applies alongside the speed threshold. Staff said volume reflects exposure to risk and the thresholds follow best practice.

On the bring-your-own events item, a councillor asked about consultation with public health and school boards. Staff said special event permits already need public health and police approval, and that the City would review its alcohol policies for parks.
